notice: Starter records only. Expand from cited sources and user-owned text. Coordinates are modern reference points, not claims that every ancient boundary or site is certain.

people_groups.name: Israelites
people_groups.period: Bronze/Iron Age biblical tradition through later Israelite/Judahite history
people_groups.note: Ancient Levantine people described in biblical and extrabiblical sources; internal tribal and regional identities varied.

people_groups.name: Judeans / Jews
people_groups.period: Especially First Temple, exilic, Second Temple, Roman and later periods
people_groups.note: Terms change across periods; “Judean” can be geographic/political while “Jew” can carry ethnic/religious dimensions.

people_groups.name: Samaritans
people_groups.note: Community centered on Mount Gerizim with Israelite heritage and its own Pentateuchal tradition.

people_groups.name: Romans
people_groups.note: Political/civic identity spanning many local peoples across the Mediterranean.

people_groups.name: Greeks / Hellenes
people_groups.period: Classical and Hellenistic eras into Roman period
people_groups.note: Language and cultural identity spread widely after Alexander; local identities remained diverse.

people_groups.name: Canaanites
people_groups.period: Bronze and early Iron Age Levant
people_groups.note: Umbrella term used in ancient texts for multiple Levantine populations/city-states; not one modern “race.”

people_groups.name: Philistines
people_groups.note: Associated with the coastal pentapolis; archaeology indicates complex Aegean and Levantine interactions.

people_groups.name: Assyrians
people_groups.note: Imperial power that conquered the northern kingdom of Israel and pressured Judah.

people_groups.name: Babylonians
people_groups.note: Empire that destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple in 587/586 BCE.

people_groups.name: Persians
people_groups.note: Imperial context for return from exile and Second Temple restoration.

people_groups.name: Egyptians
people_groups.note: A long-lived civilization whose political relationship with the Levant changed repeatedly.

persons.name: Abraham
persons.range: traditional patriarchal period; historical dating debated
persons.note: Patriarch central to Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions.

persons.name: Moses
persons.range: traditional Exodus period; historical dating debated
persons.note: Lawgiver and leader of the Exodus narrative.

persons.name: David
persons.note: King associated with Jerusalem and the Davidic dynasty.

persons.name: Hezekiah
persons.note: King of Judah during Assyrian expansion.

persons.name: Jeremiah
persons.note: Prophetic figure associated with Judah’s final decades before Babylonian conquest.

persons.name: Cyrus II of Persia
persons.note: Achaemenid ruler associated with policies permitting displaced communities to return and restore cult sites.

persons.name: Herod the Great
persons.note: Roman client king of Judea; major builder.

persons.name: Jesus of Nazareth
persons.range: born c. 6–4 BCE; death commonly dated c. 30 or 33 CE
persons.note: Central figure of Christianity. Red-letter annotation concerns reported direct speech in Gospel narrative.

persons.name: Peter
persons.note: Prominent apostle and early Christian leader.

persons.name: Paul
persons.note: Early Christian missionary and letter writer; authorship of individual epistles is discussed separately.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Ancient city; exact locations of specific structures and boundaries vary by period.

places.name: Bethlehem
places.note: Town south of Jerusalem; biblical references require passage-specific historical context.

places.name: Capernaum
places.note: Galilean lakeside settlement associated with Jesus’s ministry.

places.name: Jericho
places.note: Ancient settlement area near the Jordan Valley with multiple archaeological phases.

places.name: Rome
places.note: Capital of the Roman world and destination/context for several New Testament traditions.

places.name: Antioch on the Orontes
places.note: Major Hellenistic/Roman city near modern Antakya; important in Acts and early Christianity.

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: Major Roman city in Asia Minor.

places.name: Corinth
places.note: Greek/Roman city associated with Paul and the Corinthian correspondence.

places.name: Babylon
places.note: Ancient Mesopotamian city; “Babylon” can also function symbolically in later texts such as Revelation.

objects.name: Ark of the Covenant
objects.note: Sacred chest described in Torah narratives; no securely identified surviving artifact.

objects.name: Tabernacle
objects.note: Portable sanctuary in Pentateuchal narrative; descriptions have major theological and ritual importance.

objects.name: Jerusalem Temple
objects.note: First and Second Temple periods must be distinguished; Herodian expansion belongs to the Second Temple period.

objects.name: Ephod
objects.note: Priestly object/garment described in Exodus and other texts; exact reconstruction is debated.

objects.name: Denarius
objects.note: Roman silver coin appearing in New Testament contexts; purchasing power varies by time/place.

objects.name: Synagogue
objects.note: Jewish communal/scriptural institution with varied forms in the Second Temple and Roman periods.

timeline.label: United monarchy / early Davidic dynasty (conventional chronology)
Destruction of Jerusalem and First Temple
Second Temple completion (conventional)
timeline.note: Dating convention varies by calendar/regnal reckoning.

timeline.label: Roman intervention in Judea under Pompey
timeline.note: Jerusalem enters Roman sphere of dominance.

timeline.label: Public ministry of Jesus (approximate)
timeline.note: Chronologies commonly place the ministry in the late 20s/early 30s CE.

timeline.label: Pauline mission and correspondence
timeline.note: Individual journeys and letters have more specific proposed dates.

timeline.label: Destruction of Second Temple
timeline.note: Roman destruction during the First Jewish Revolt.
